The backbone of virtually all modern large language models traces back to the **Transformer architecture**, introduced by Google in 2017, but several major variants and alternatives have since emerged. Understanding these backbone architectures means understanding how information flows from input tokens to generated outputs.
## The Transformer: The Core Blueprint
The original Transformer solved a critical problem that plagued earlier sequence models like RNNs: the inability to capture long-range dependencies efficiently. It does this through a mechanism called **self-attention**, which allows every token in a sequence to directly "look at" every other token simultaneously, rather than processing sequentially. The architecture is built from stacked layers, each containing a multi-head attention block followed by a feed-forward neural network (FFNN), with normalization layers in between. Positional encodings inject word-order information since the attention mechanism itself is order-agnostic.[1][2]
## Encoder-Only Models
Encoder-only architectures, like **BERT** and **RoBERTa**, use only the left half of the original Transformer. The encoder reads the full input sequence bidirectionally — meaning every token attends to all others simultaneously — producing rich contextual embeddings of the input. Because both left and right context is available at every position, these models develop a deep, nuanced understanding of text. They excel at classification, named entity recognition, and semantic search, but they are not designed to generate new text.[3][4]
## Decoder-Only Models
Decoder-only models like the **GPT series**, **LLaMA**, and **Claude** are the dominant architecture for generative AI today. They use **causal (masked) self-attention**, meaning each token can only attend to tokens that came before it — processing left to right, one token at a time. This autoregressive design makes them natural text generators: they predict the next token given all previous tokens, and repeat until a full response is formed. Because they never see future context during training, their representations are inherently directional, which suits open-ended generation, question answering, and chat.[5][6]
## Encoder-Decoder (Seq2Seq) Models
Encoder-Decoder models like **T5** and **BART** use both halves of the original Transformer. The encoder reads and compresses the full input into a rich representation, and the decoder generates the output sequence guided by that representation via cross-attention. This design is ideal when the output must be semantically tied to but structurally different from the input — tasks like machine translation, summarization, and document-conditioned Q&A. T5, famously, reformulates every NLP task as a text-to-text problem, feeding the same architecture regardless of task type.[3][7]

| Architecture | Attention Style | Key Models | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encoder-Only | Bidirectional | BERT, RoBERTa | Classification, embeddings |
| Decoder-Only | Causal (left-to-right) | GPT-4, LLaMA, Claude | Generation, chat |
| Encoder-Decoder | Both | T5, BART | Translation, summarization |
## State Space Models (SSMs) & Mamba
A compelling non-Transformer backbone is the **State Space Model (SSM)** family, with **Mamba** as its most prominent modern incarnation. Standard Transformers have quadratic complexity in sequence length because every token attends to every other — this becomes expensive for very long contexts. Mamba addresses this with linear complexity by modeling sequences as continuous-time dynamical systems, maintaining a compressed "state" that evolves as new tokens arrive. Its key innovation is a **selective mechanism**: unlike earlier SSMs with fixed parameters, Mamba's state transition matrices adapt based on input content, allowing it to selectively focus on relevant information and filter out noise. This makes Mamba particularly attractive for long-document processing and streaming applications.[8][9][10]
## Mixture of Experts (MoE)
The **Mixture of Experts** architecture is not a replacement for Transformers but a powerful extension of them. Instead of a single monolithic feed-forward network in each Transformer layer, MoE replaces it with many "expert" sub-networks plus a **router** that decides which experts handle which tokens. Critically, only a sparse subset of experts activates per token — for example, Mixtral 8x7B uses 8 experts per layer but activates only 2 per token. This allows the total parameter count (and thus model capacity) to scale dramatically without a proportional increase in compute, since most parameters stay dormant for any given input. Models like **Mixtral**, **Grok**, and **DeepSeek** all use sparse MoE backbones.[11][12]
